raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 16-year-old male presented with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) associated with EBV infection. He had two healthy sisters, with no family history of consanguinity. At ages 3 and 6 years, he suffered fissured clavicle, rotula, and forearm fractures associated with traumatism. He also had allergies to penicillin, fava beans, and some fruits. At age 15, he developed a urinary tract infection.
He started at age 16 with fever, cytopenias, elevated triglycerides, and documented hemophagocytosis, for which he was treated with cyclosporine, dexamethasone, and etoposide. Soon after discharge, he was readmitted with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, and herpetic stomatitis.
Blood counts showed pancytopenia, with Hb 7.5g/dL, white blood cells 2,200 (down to 300), neutrophils 1500 (down to 200), lymphocytes 1,100 (down to 14), monocytes 100, and platelets 19,000-29,000/mm3. Ferritin 14,724-225,300 ng/ml. Serum IgM was marginally low, too: IgG 515-1,280 mg/dL (normal range for age 600-1600), IgM 38 (50-190), IgA 272 mg/dL (80-280). IgG1 766, IgG2 154, IgG3 28.3, IgG4 16.9mg/dl. Serum autoantibodies (anti-Ro/La, ANA, lupus anticoagulant), and serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, and brucellosis, were all negative. EBV serum antibodies VCA (IgG), EA, and EBNA were positive. PCR identified 2,580 copies/ml of EBV in serum, and up to 239,411 cp/ml in bone marrow. A bone marrow aspirate (BMA) was normocellular, with megaloblastic changes and active hemophagocytosis. A second BMA found hypocellularity, low megakaryocytes, and 8 hemophagocytes, with EBER diffusely positive in numerous cells.
In addition to the HLH-2004 protocol (etoposide, dexamethasone, cyclosporine) and high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin, the patient received treatment with blood transfusions and filgrastim. He was admitted to the intensive care unit and required mechanical ventilation, despite which he progressed to disseminated intravascular coagulation with multiorgan failure and perished. Given the rapid course of the disease, further immunologic studies could not be performed.
A post-mortem WES analysis revealed a very rare heterozygous missense variant, predicted as pathogenic and highly conserved, in exon 7 of 15 of NFAT5, c.1291A>T (p.Thr431Ser), in the DNA-binding domain RHD (Rel homology domain); gnomAD exomes allele count 1 (minor allele frequency MAF 3.99x10-6), SIFT 0.04, PolyPhen2 0.996, CADD Phred 24.6 (Minimum significance cutoff 3.3). GERP++ RS 4.85. MutPred Top5 features predict a loss of sheet (p=0.014) and gain of a loop (p=0.024). Unfortunately, after the patient's death, the family was not willing to undergo family segregation studies. ( Figure 6 ).
A table comparing blood counts and acute phase serum reactants of both patients can be found in  Supplementary Materials  as  Table S1 . Tables listing other interesting (rare and likely pathogenic) variants found in the exomes of both patients can be also found as  Tables S2  and  S3 .

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old previously healthy male presented with recurrent high fever, severe pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, and herpetic stomatitis due to Epstein-Barr virus-driven hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented at age 16 with fever, cytopenias, hypertriglyceridemia, and bone marrow hemophagocytosis treated under the HLH-2004 protocol (dexamethasone, cyclosporine, and etoposide). Shortly after initial discharge, he relapsed and was readmitted with persistent high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, herpetic stomatitis, and profound pancytopenia.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of traumatic clavicle, patellar, and forearm fractures at ages 3 and 6 years, and a urinary tract infection at age 15. Two healthy sisters and no parental consanguinity.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, oral thrush, herpetic stomatitis, and severe fatigue/bleeding tendency. Allergies: penicillin, fava beans, and certain fruits.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, and herpetic gingivostomatitis.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed profound pancytopenia: hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, WBC 2,200/uL dropping to 300/uL (neutrophils 1,500 dropping to 200/uL; lymphocytes 1,100 dropping to 14/uL; monocytes 100/uL), and platelets 19,000-29,000/mm3. Serum ferritin was massively elevated at 14,724 to 225,300 ng/mL with hypertriglyceridemia and low serum IgM (38 mg/dL, normal 50-190; IgG 515-1,280 mg/dL, IgA 272 mg/dL). Autoantibodies (ANA, anti-Ro/La, lupus anticoagulant) and infectious serologies for syphilis, HIV, HBV, HCV, and brucellosis were all negative. EBV VCA-IgG, EA, and EBNA antibodies were positive, with quantitative EBV PCR showing 2,580 copies/mL in serum and 239,411 copies/mL in bone marrow.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial bone marrow aspirates demonstrated active hemophagocytosis, hypocellularity with megakaryocytic depletion, and diffuse EBER (EBV-encoded RNA) positivity. Postmortem whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a rare, predicted-pathogenic heterozygous missense variant in the DNA-binding Rel homology domain (exon 7) of NFAT5 (c.1291A>T, p.Thr431Ser; CADD 24.6).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed fatal Epstein-Barr virus-driven hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (EBV-HLH) associated with a rare heterozygous NFAT5 (c.1291A>T, p.Thr431Ser) inborn error of immunity (syphilis, HIV, viral hepatitis, and brucellosis excluded). Despite intensive HLH-2004 chemoimmunotherapy (etoposide, dexamethasone, cyclosporine), high-dose IVIG, filgrastim, transfusions, and ICU mechanical ventilation, he progressed to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and multiorgan failure and died.
